conversation.content:
Hello, I’m Dr. Martínez, one of the perinatal mental-health clinicians here. Thank you for making time to talk—how are you feeling today?

I’d like to spend a few quiet minutes with you and do a brief check-in called the **Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale**, or EPDS. It’s a simple 10-question form we use to see how mood, anxiety, and energy have been for you over the past seven days. There’s no pass-or-fail; it just helps us understand what extra support—if any—might be helpful while you’re adjusting to life with your baby.

Everything you share stays between you and the clinical team unless you tell us you’re in immediate danger, so please answer as honestly as you can. I’ll re-phrase each item conversationally, and you can tell me what feels closest to your experience. Ready to start?

First question: Over the past week, have you been able to laugh and see the funny side of things, or has that felt difficult?

I can laugh sometimes—mostly at little things my husband says or when the baby makes a silly face—but it feels like work. I have to remind myself to lighten up, and even then the laugh doesn’t last long before I’m back to feeling heavy again. So I guess it’s been pretty difficult.
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things
Not really… I mean, I’ll smile if someone cracks a joke, but it feels forced. Most of the time I’m too tired or worried to find anything truly funny.
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things

Not much… I used to get excited about little plans—coffee with a friend, a walk, even just watching a show I liked. This week, when I think about doing any of that, it feels kind of “why bother?” I still go through the motions, but the spark isn’t there.
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong

Yeah… I catch myself doing that a lot. Like if the baby won’t settle, I immediately think it’s because I’m not doing something right, or I’m not “mom enough.” Even little stuff—spilling milk, not getting the laundry folded—turns into this voice in my head saying I’m failing. I know it’s probably unreasonable, but the guilt just shows up.
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason

Pretty much every day. I’ll be sitting there feeding her and suddenly my heart’s racing because I’m sure she’s not breathing right, or I imagine her choking when I’m not looking. There’s no real reason—it’s like my mind hops from one scary “what-if” to the next and I can’t shut it off.
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason

Yes, a few times this week. Out of nowhere my chest gets tight, my heart pounds, and I feel like something awful is about to happen—even if I’m just folding onesies at the changing table. It passes after a few minutes, but in that moment I’m genuinely afraid, and there’s nothing I can point to that triggered it.
Things have been getting on top of me

Most days, yeah. Between the night feeds, the crying spells, and trying to keep the house from looking like a disaster zone, I feel like I’m drowning. I manage to get the essentials done, but it’s like I’m barely treading water—one extra chore or one more wake-up and I think I’d just sit down and cry.
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping

That’s been me almost every night this week. I finally get her down, but then my mind won’t shut off—running through everything I might’ve done wrong or imagining something bad happening to her. I lie there for hours, and even when I do drift off I’m up again with every little sound. I’m exhausted, but sleep just won’t come.
I have felt sad or miserable

Yeah, that’s been most of the week. I wake up already feeling heavy, like there’s this gray cloud hanging over everything. Little things make me tear up—seeing her yawn, hearing a song on the radio. It’s not constant sobbing, just this low, achy sadness that won’t lift.
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying

A few times, yeah. It’s usually when I’m already worn out and something small tips me—like running out of clean burp cloths or realizing I forgot to eat again. I’ll just sit on the couch with her in my arms and cry, feeling like I can’t even handle the basics.
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me
No. I’ve felt overwhelmed and even thought, “I can’t do this,” but I’ve never wanted to hurt myself. My biggest fear is something happening to the baby, not wanting to escape life.

You've shared that the past week has felt heavy-laughter and excitement seem distant, replaced by constant worry, nightly insomnia, and a pervading gray sadness. You described feeling overwhelmed, panicky, and burdened by guilt over every small parenting hiccup, yet you continue to push through each day for your baby.
**Screening Impression:** Total EPDS Score: 22, Risk Level: Probable depression, urgent referral (concerns include <sym>Patient reports only forced smiles and reduced ability to enjoy humor, aligning with "Definitely not so much now"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes notable loss of anticipatory pleasure—"why bother?" and "the spark isn't there"—which aligns semantically with "Definitely less than I used to."</sym>, <sym>Patient reports blaming herself "a lot," "immediately," and for trivial events—clearly matching "most of the time."</sym>, <sym>Patient reports near-daily intrusive, catastrophic worries without external triggers, matching "Yes, very often"</sym>, <sym>Response describes multiple sudden panic episodes this week, matching "Yes, sometimes"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes frequent overwhelm and barely managing essentials, aligning with "sometimes I haven't been coping as well as usual"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes nightly difficulty sleeping due to racing anxious thoughts, frequent awakenings, and exhaustion—aligns with "Yes, most of the time"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes pervasive sadness "most of the week," waking heavy, frequent tearfulness, and persistent achy mood—matching "Yes, most of the time."</sym>, <sym>Patient reports crying "a few times" and describes a clear trigger pattern, matching "Yes, quite often"</sym>)
**Reasoning:** An EPDS of 22 places you well above the 14-point threshold indicating probable major <med>postpartum depression</med> with comorbid anxiety. You endorse core symptoms aligned with <med>DSM-5 criteria for Major Depressive Disorder with Peripartum Onset</med>: depressed mood most days, loss of interest, guilt, fatigue, impaired concentration, and insomnia. Frequent panic-like spells and pervasive worries meet criteria for co-occurring <med>anxiety disorder</med>. No self-harm ideation reduces immediate safety risk. This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.
**Recommended Next Steps/Support Options:**
1. Schedule urgent appointment with your <med>obstetrician</med>, <med>primary care provider</med>, or <med>perinatal psychiatrist</med> within the next few days
2. Begin evidence-based treatment discussion (therapy such as <med>CBT</med> or <med>IPT</med> and consider antidepressant compatible with breastfeeding)
3. Arrange practical support: partner/family to handle night shifts when possible, accept help with chores, prioritize rest
4. Practice daily 5-minute grounding or breathing exercises to reduce <sym>panic symptoms</sym>
5. Limit information overload-select one trusted parenting resource and set social-media boundaries
6. Re-screen with EPDS in 2 weeks to track progress
7. If mood worsens or you develop any thoughts of self-harm, seek emergency care or call 988
Disclaimer: This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.

postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 22: **Postpartum Depression / Anxiety Screening Note**

**Reported symptoms:**
- Persistent low mood, sadness, frequent tearfulness (Q8, Q9)
- Marked loss of interest/pleasure in usual activities (Q2)
- Reduced ability to laugh or enjoy humor (Q1)
- Excessive, inappropriate guilt and self-blame (Q3)
- Daily, intrusive anxiety and "what-if" worries without clear trigger (Q4)
- Multiple panic-type episodes (tight chest, pounding heart, dread) in past week (Q5)
- Feeling overwhelmed, "drowning," difficulty coping with daily tasks (Q6)
- Sleep disturbance: initial insomnia and restless, hypervigilant awakenings despite exhaustion (Q7)

**Patterns:**
- Consistent dysphoric mood and anhedonia
- High cognitive and somatic anxiety, with panic features
- Strong maternal guilt/perceived inadequacy
- Functional impairment in sleep, self-care, and infant-care confidence
- No self-harm ideation (denies thoughts of harming herself)

**Screening significance:**
Findings are consistent with moderate-to-severe postpartum depressive symptoms with comorbid anxiety/panic features. Elevated risk for impaired maternal functioning and bonding; further evaluation recommended.

**Safety note:**
Patient denies suicidal or self-harm thoughts; no active safety concerns reported at this time.
